entry: American financier and philanthropist. The only son of Standard Oil co-founder [[John D. Rockefeller]], he was involved in developing Rockefeller Center in [[Manhattan]], making him one of the largest real estate holders in New York City at that time. Toward the end of his life he gave over $500 million to a wide range of causes, including educational institutions, and his projects included the reconstruction of Colonial Williamsburg in [[Virginia]]. He was widely blamed for the Ludlow Massacre during the Colorado Coalfield War.

English chemist, physicist, and meteorologist. He proposed that each chemical element consists of identical [[Atom|atoms]] of characteristic weight, and that compounds form when atoms of different elements combine in fixed whole-number proportions. Building on earlier ideas about the indivisibility of matter, his work laid the foundations of modern atomic theory and stoichiometric chemistry. His *A New System of Chemical Philosophy* (1808) presented a coherent atomic model and supplied relative atomic weights and symbolic notation. He formulated the first empirical law of partial [[Pressure|pressures]], later known as Dalton's law, and he kept daily weather observations for over fifty years. He also rediscovered George Hadley's theory of atmospheric circulation, now known as the [[Hadley cell]]. His investigations into his own [[Color blindness|color blindness]] produced the first scientific description of the condition, which in several languages is still known as Daltonism.

American singer, songwriter, and actor. One of the most popular acoustic artists of the 1970s, he recorded roughly 300 songs, about 200 of which he wrote himself. His songs, including "Take Me Home, Country Roads" and "Rocky Mountain High," often focused on nature, music, and relationships. Known for his love of [[Colorado]], he was named poet laureate of the state in 1974, and West Virginia adopted "Take Me Home, Country Roads" as a state song in 2014. He starred with [[George Burns]] in the 1977 film *Oh, God!* He died in a single-fatality crash while piloting a light plane he had just bought.

American philosopher, psychologist, and educational reformer. The overriding theme of his work was belief in [[Democracy|democracy]] in politics, education, and communication and [[Journalism|journalism]]. He argued that complete democracy required not just voting rights but also a fully formed public opinion, created through communication among citizens, experts, and politicians. He was a primary figure in [[Pragmatism|pragmatism]] and one of the founding thinkers of functional psychology; his 1896 paper "The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology" is regarded as the first major work of the Chicago functionalist school. A 2002 survey ranked him the 93rd-most-cited psychologist of the 20th century. While a professor at the [[University of Chicago]], he founded the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools to test progressive ideas on pedagogical method. From 1904 until his retirement in 1930 he was professor of philosophy at Teachers College, Columbia University. He also wrote on [[Epistemology|epistemology]], [[Metaphysics|metaphysics]], aesthetics, logic, and ethics.

American gangster and bank robber. He commanded the Dillinger Gang during the Great Depression, which was accused of robbing 24 banks and four police stations. The media printed exaggerated accounts of his bravado and described him as a [[Robin Hood]]-type figure. In response, [[J. Edgar Hoover]] used the case to justify evolving the Bureau of Investigation into the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]], developing investigative techniques against [[Organized crime|organized crime]]. He escaped custody twice and was charged with, but never convicted of, the murder of an East Chicago, Indiana, police officer. Federal agents fatally shot him outside the Biograph Theater in [[Chicago]].

English poet and cleric. Born into a recusant Roman Catholic family, Donne could not earn a degree at Oxford or at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]] because he refused to take the Oath of Supremacy. He is considered the preeminent representative of the metaphysical poets. His style features abrupt openings and various [[Paradox|paradoxes]], ironies, and dislocations, and he is known for his mastery of metaphysical conceits. His works include [[Sonnet|sonnets]], love and religious poems, Latin translations, elegies, and satires, as well as sermons. He secretly married Anne More and lived in poverty for several years, relying on wealthy friends. In 1615 he was unwillingly ordained an Anglican deacon and then priest at the king's insistence. Under royal patronage he was made Dean of St Paul's Cathedral in [[City of London|London]] (1621–1631). His brother Henry died in Newgate Prison of [[Bubonic plague|bubonic plague]] after his arrest in 1593 for harboring a Catholic priest.

English poet, literary critic, translator, and playwright. Dryden was appointed England's first Poet Laureate in 1668, and he dominated the literary life of the Restoration to such a point that the period came to be known in literary circles as the Age of Dryden. His "Heroic Stanzas" (1659) eulogized [[Oliver Cromwell]] in cautious terms, and after the Restoration he celebrated Charles II in "Astraea Redux." His political [[Satire|satire]] *Absalom and Achitophel* (1681) defended Charles II in heroic couplets. His plays included *All for Love* (1678), a reworking of Shakespeare's *Antony and Cleopatra*. He converted to Roman Catholicism around 1685, and he lost the laureateship after the [[Glorious Revolution]] because he refused to take the oath to William III and Mary II. He then supported himself with translations of classical authors such as [[Virgil]]. He was buried in [[Westminster Abbey]].

American football quarterback and executive. Elway played 16 seasons for the Denver Broncos of the [[National Football League]]. He was taken first in the 1983 draft by the Baltimore Colts and immediately traded to Denver. In January 1987 he helped engineer a 98-yard, game-tying touchdown drive in the AFC Championship Game, later dubbed "The Drive." The Broncos won back-to-back [[Super Bowl|Super Bowls]], and Elway was named MVP of Super Bowl XXXIII. He later became general manager, and the team won Super Bowl 50 during his tenure. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2004.

International airport in [[Queens]], [[New York City]]. It is the busiest of the three airports in the New York system and the sixth-busiest in the United States. Covering 5,200 acres (2,104 ha), it is the largest airport in the New York metropolitan area, and nearly 100 airlines operate from it. It has five passenger terminals and four runways. [[American Airlines]] and [[Delta Air Lines]] are hubs, and JetBlue has its primary operating base there. The facility opened in 1948 as New York International Airport, commonly known as Idlewild Airport, and was renamed in late 1963 in tribute to President [[John F. Kennedy]].

35th [[President of the United States|president of the United States]] (1961–63). A Democrat from Massachusetts, he was the first Roman Catholic president. He narrowly defeated [[Richard Nixon]] in 1960. He increased the number of American military advisers in South Vietnam, and in 1961 he authorized an attempt to overthrow Fidel Castro's Cuban government, the failed [[Bay of Pigs Invasion]]. After U.S. spy planes found Soviet missile bases in Cuba in October 1962, the [[Cuban Missile Crisis]] nearly led to nuclear war. After East German troops erected the [[Berlin Wall]], he sent an army convoy to reassure West Berliners of U.S. support. He presided over the creation of the Peace Corps and the [[Apollo program]], which aimed to land a man on the Moon before 1970. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas. The Warren Commission concluded that [[Lee Harvey Oswald]] acted alone, but conspiracy theories persist.

American mathematician and Nobel laureate. As a graduate student at [[Princeton University]], he introduced the [[Nash equilibrium]], a concept now central to [[Game theory|game theory]]. He shared the 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences and, in 2015, the Abel Prize. In the 1950s he proved the Nash embedding theorems by solving nonlinear partial differential equations arising in [[Riemannian geometry]]. From 1959 he showed signs of mental illness and spent several years in [[Psychiatric hospital|psychiatric hospitals]], treated for [[Schizophrenia]]. He returned to academic work by the mid-1980s. His struggles inspired the 2001 film *A Beautiful Mind*, directed by [[Ron Howard]], with [[Russell Crowe]] as Nash.

American film director and producer. He is regarded as one of the most important filmmakers of the Golden Age of Hollywood and one of the first American directors recognized as an *auteur*. He directed more than 130 films and won a record four [[Academy Awards]] for Best Director, for *The Informer* (1935), *The Grapes of Wrath* (1940), *How Green Was My Valley* (1941), and *The Quiet Man* (1952). Ford is renowned for Westerns such as *Stagecoach* (1939), *The Searchers* (1956), and *The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance* (1962). He launched the careers of [[John Wayne]], [[Henry Fonda]], and [[James Stewart]]. Directors including [[Akira Kurosawa]], [[Orson Welles]], [[Frank Capra]], and [[Ingmar Bergman]] named him among the greatest directors of all time.

English actor and theater director. With [[Laurence Olivier]], Michael Redgrave, and Ralph Richardson, he was one of four male actors who dominated the British stage in the mid-20th century. He was famous for his voice and his mastery of Shakespearean verse, and many regarded him as the finest Hamlet of his era. In the 1950s he was convicted and fined for a homosexual offense, but his colleagues and the public supported him. He won an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor as the acid-tongued Hobson in *Arthur* (1981) and is one of few performers to have won an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar, and a Tony. He began a parallel career as a director and set up his own company at the Queen's Theatre, London. He was knighted in 1953.

American mobster. Gotti ordered the December 1985 murder of Gambino boss Paul Castellano and took over the family, which was described as the most powerful crime syndicate in the United States. He was called the "Teflon Don" after three high-profile 1980s trials ended in acquittals, later revealed to have been tainted by jury tampering and witness intimidation. His underboss, Salvatore Gravano, aided the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] and testified against him, and in 1992 Gotti was convicted of five murders, racketeering, and other crimes. He received [[Life imprisonment|life imprisonment]] without parole and died of [[Cancer|throat cancer]] at a federal medical center in [[Missouri|Springfield, Missouri]].

American writer and lawyer. Known for best-selling legal thrillers, he has written 37 consecutive number-one fiction bestsellers, according to the American Academy of Achievement, and his books have sold 300 million copies worldwide. He practiced criminal law for about a decade and served in the [[Mississippi]] House of Representatives from 1983 to 1990. His first bestseller, *The Firm*, sold more than seven million copies and was adapted into a 1993 film starring [[Tom Cruise]]. He is one of three Anglophone authors, with [[Tom Clancy]] and [[J. K. Rowling]], to have sold two million copies on the first printing.

American pornographic film actor. He appeared as Johnny Wadd in a series of films and is among the most famous and prolific adult film performers, with documented credits for at least 573 films. His marketing heavily promoted his physical endowment. Near the end of his life he was charged over his reputed involvement in the Wonderland murders of July 1981, and he was later acquitted. He died of complications from AIDS. He was the subject of several books and a lengthy essay in *Rolling Stone*, and he inspired two Hollywood films, *Boogie Nights* (1997) and *Wonderland* (2003).

American filmmaker, writer, and producer. Best known for 1980s coming-of-age comedies such as *Sixteen Candles* (1984), *The Breakfast Club* (1985), and *Ferris Bueller's Day Off* (1986), he set most of his films in [[Chicago]], where he spent his teenage years. His early career included selling jokes to [[Rodney Dangerfield]] and [[Joan Rivers]]. He also wrote *Planes, Trains and Automobiles* (1987) and *Home Alone* (1990), and his work often combined slapstick comedy with heartfelt moments.

Hungarian military and political figure. As regent of the [[Kingdom of Hungary]] from 1446 to 1453, during the minority of Ladislaus V, he was the leading Hungarian figure of the 15th century. Contemporaries nicknamed him "Turk-buster," and he defended the southern frontier against the [[Ottoman Empire]]. In 1442 he won the Battle of the Ialomița, the first time a European army had defeated such a large Ottoman force. His victories motivated the successful Long Campaign of 1443–1444, but his later crusade ended in defeat at Varna in 1444. In 1456 he won the Siege of [[Belgrade]] against an army led by Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror, halting Ottoman expansion beyond the Balkans for 70 years. Christian church bells are rung at noon to commemorate the victory. He died weeks later of an epidemic, and his fame helped elect his son, [[Matthias Corvinus]], king in 1457.

English actor. Regarded as one of the finest actors of his generation, he received [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations for *Midnight Express* (1978) and *The Elephant Man* (1980). His career took off in the mid-1970s, with *The Naked Civil Servant* (1975) and the role of Caligula in the [[BBC]] series *I, Claudius* (1976). He played Garrick Ollivander in the [[Harry Potter (film series)|Harry Potter]] films, portrayed the War Doctor in [[Doctor Who]], and was knighted in 2015. He was described as having the "most distinctive voice in Britain."

American-Irish filmmaker and actor. He directed 37 feature films, many now considered classics, and wrote the screenplays for many of them. His films include *The Maltese Falcon* (1941), *The Treasure of the Sierra Madre* (1948), *The African Queen* (1951), and *Prizzi's Honor* (1985). He won two [[Academy Awards]] and was the only director in Academy history to guide both his father and his daughter, [[Anjelica Huston]], to Oscar acting wins. He acted in films including [[Chinatown (1974 film)|Chinatown]] (1974) and voiced the wizard [[Gandalf]] in *The Hobbit* (1977). He settled in France, Mexico, and Ireland, and became an Irish citizen in 1964.

King of Poland and grand duke of Lithuania (1674–96). Born into Polish nobility, he fought in the Khmelnytsky Uprising, the Russo-Polish War, and the Swedish invasion known as the Deluge. He then proved his military ability against the [[Ottoman Empire]]. He was elected monarch of the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]] in 1674 after the sudden death of King Michael Korybut Wiśniowiecki. The reign marked a period of stabilization for the Commonwealth. His most famous victory was at the [[Battle of Vienna]] in 1683, after which the defeated Ottomans called him the "Lion of Lechistan" and the pope hailed him as savior of Western Christendom. Suffering from poor health and obesity in later life, he was buried at Wawel Cathedral in [[Kraków]] and succeeded by [[Augustus II the Strong]].

United States Army general. Nicknamed "Black Jack," he commanded the American Expeditionary Forces in [[World War I]] from 1917 to 1920. He insisted that the AEF operate as a single unit under his command rather than be integrated with British or French armies. For the Meuse-Argonne Offensive he shifted roughly 600,000 American soldiers to the Argonne forests, keeping his divisions in hard fighting for 47 days. He was the only American promoted in his lifetime to General of the Armies, the highest rank in the U.S. Army. Pershing mentored many of the generals who led in [[World War II]], including [[George C. Marshall]], [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]], [[George S. Patton]], and [[Douglas MacArthur]]. Historians have blamed his reliance on costly frontal assaults for unnecessarily high American casualties, and he maintained that he had followed the orders of his superior, [[Ferdinand Foch]].

French-American artist, naturalist, and ornithologist. Born in Saint-Domingue (now [[Haiti]]), he was raised in Couëron, near [[Nantes]], France. His best-known work, *The Birds of America* (1827–1838), is a double-elephant folio of hand-colored plates engraved in Scotland and England. Its 435 plates depict 489 North American bird species, produced at great personal financial risk. His illustrations emphasized behavior and environment over the stiff poses of taxidermy, and he studied birds during extensive travels across the continent. He was accused of fraud, [[Plagiarism|plagiarism]], and scientific misconduct during his life and afterward. He is also widely criticized for buying and selling enslaved people, body snatching, and trafficking Native American remains.

English Romantic poet. Writing alongside [[Lord Byron]] and [[Percy Bysshe Shelley]] in the second generation of Romantic poets, he developed a style "heavily loaded with sensualities," notably in his odes. His poems had been in publication for less than four years when he died of [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]] at 25, and they were indifferently received in his lifetime. His fame grew rapidly after his death, and by the end of the century he was placed in the canon of English literature. Today his poems and letters remain among the most popular and analyzed in English literature, including "Ode to a Nightingale" and "Ode on a Grecian Urn." His medievalist poems, such as "La Belle Dame sans Merci," influenced the [[Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood|Pre-Raphaelite movement]]. He died in [[Rome]].

Canadian-American economist and diplomat. A long-time [[Harvard University|Harvard]] professor, he wrote four dozen books, including the trilogy *American Capitalism* (1952), *The Affluent Society* (1958), and *The New Industrial State* (1967). During World War II he was deputy director of the Office of Price Administration, in charge of stabilizing prices, wages, and rents. He served in the administrations of [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]], [[Harry S. Truman]], [[John F. Kennedy]], and [[Lyndon B. Johnson]], and as ambassador to India under Kennedy. He was influenced by [[John Maynard Keynes]] during a fellowship at the [[University of Cambridge]]. He received the World War II Medal of Freedom (1946) and the Presidential Medal of Freedom (2000). Critics, including George Stigler, argued that concepts such as countervailing power lacked empirical support.
